title: On the Morning of Christ's Nativity
description: Milton's first major poem, written at twenty-one: a hymn celebrating the Incarnation, in which the birth of Christ brings universal peace and harmony, silencing the oracles and the pagan gods and summoning a heavenly music that the poet longs to join.
plot_or_argument: A prologue in four stanzas asks whether the poet's verse may be laid in the manger before the Magi; the Hymn then describes the peaceful night, the music of the spheres, and the flight of the pagan deities (Apollo, Osiris, Typhon) before the true God.
narrative_structure: A four-stanza prologue followed by an irregular Pindaric-style Hymn in varied stanza form, moving from celebration to the rout of the old gods.
principal_characters: the poet; the infant Christ; Nature; Peace; the pagan gods (Apollo, Osiris, Typhon)
meter_and_prosody: Prologue in rhyme royal; the Hymn in a complex varied stanza (aabbcccddedeeff) that Milton devised for the occasion.
historical_context: Composed in December 1629, the year Milton took his MA at Cambridge; published in his Poems of Mr. John Milton (1645), where it leads the collection as his claim to a great poetic vocation.
literary_significance: A precocious masterpiece of the early English baroque, it announces Milton's ambition to Christian epic and his fusion of classical and biblical learning.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; dated by Milton himself in the 1645 volume.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Poems of Mr. John Milton (1645). Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: L'Allegro and Il Penseroso
description: A pair of companion poems contrasting two temperaments and ways of life: L'Allegro celebrates the active, social, cheerful mirth of the day and the countryside, while Il Penseroso praises the contemplative, melancholic, studious and religious delights of night and solitude.
plot_or_argument: L'Allegro banishes melancholy and summons Mirth, tracing a day of rustic and urban pleasures culminating in music and masque; Il Penseroso banishes vain deluding joys and invokes 'pensive Nun', tracing a life of study, woodland meditation, church music, and a hoped-for prophetic vision.
narrative_structure: Two matched lyrics in alternating tetrameter and pentameter couplets, structured as a balanced debate between the active and contemplative lives.
principal_characters: the poet; Mirth (Euphrosyne); Melancholy; the pensive Nun (Contemplation)
meter_and_prosody: Mixed tetrameter and pentameter couplets with varied lyric effects; the two poems mirror each other in structure.
historical_context: Written during Milton's years of private study at Horton (c. 1632), published in the 1645 Poems; they reflect the Renaissance contrast of the active and contemplative lives.
literary_significance: Among the most admired of Milton's shorter poems, they established his command of the English lyric and became models for eighteenth-century descriptive and meditative verse.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Poems of Mr. John Milton (1645). Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Comus (A Masque Presented at Ludlow Castle)
description: A masque written for the installation of the Earl of Bridgewater as Lord President of Wales and performed at Ludlow Castle on Michaelmas night 1634: the Lady, separated from her brothers, is tempted by the sorcerer Comus to sensual pleasure but preserves her chastity through steadfast virtue, and is freed by the Attendant Spirit and Sabrina.
plot_or_argument: Comus ensnares the Lady with an enchanter's cup, immobilising her body while her mind remains free; her brothers and the Attendant Spirit rout Comus, and the water-nymph Sabrina releases the Lady, who is presented to her parents.
narrative_structure: A masque in blank verse and song, with a moral-allegorical debate between the Lady and Comus, a masque-typical resolution by a deity, and a concluding song and epilogue.
principal_characters: the Lady; Comus; the two Brothers; the Attendant Spirit (Thyrsis); Sabrina
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse interspersed with lyric songs; a grave, elevated style unusual for the court masque.
historical_context: Composed in 1634 with music by Henry Lawes, who played the Attendant Spirit; it adapts the court masque to a serious moral and Puritan-inflected theme of chastity.
literary_significance: Milton's longest early poem and a transformation of the masque into serious moral poetry; its celebration of chastity and virtue anticipates the ethical concerns of Paradise Lost.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; published anonymously in 1637, then in the 1645 Poems under Milton's name.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1637. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Lycidas
description: Milton's pastoral elegy for Edward King, a Cambridge contemporary drowned off the Irish coast in 1637, written for the memorial volume Justa Edouardo King; it mourns the young poet's death, indicts the corrupt clergy, and consoles with the promise of resurrection and fame in heaven.
plot_or_argument: The shepherd-poet mourns Lycidas, questions divine justice, invokes the Muse and St Peter (who denounces the 'blind mouths' of the corrupt church), hears the tale of Lycidas's drowning and apotheosis, and finds consolation in the belief that he is 'sunk low, but mounted high' as the genius of the shore.
narrative_structure: A pastoral elegy in irregular verse, moving from grief and doubt through the prophetic denunciation by St Peter to Christian consolation and the poet's turn to 'pastures new'.
principal_characters: the uncouth swain (Milton); Lycidas (Edward King); St Peter; the Muse; Jove
meter_and_prosody: A varied and intricately rhymed pastoral stanza of irregular line lengths, with carefully placed short lines and refrains.
historical_context: Written in 1637 for the collection Justa Edouardo King Naufrago (1638); it draws on the pastoral elegiac tradition from Theocritus and Virgil to Spenser, transfigured by Milton's Puritan faith and anticlerical anger.
literary_significance: Widely regarded as the greatest pastoral elegy in English, Lycidas combines personal grief, political and religious satire, and visionary consolation in a uniquely wrought form.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; signed 'J.M.' in the 1638 volume and included in the 1645 Poems.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Justa Edouardo King Naufrago (1638). Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Milton's Sonnets
description: Milton's twenty-four English and five Italian sonnets, written over some thirty years: a sequence of public and private meditations including 'How soon hath Time', 'On His Blindness' ('When I consider how my light is spent'), the political sonnets 'On the Late Massacre at Piemont' and 'To the Lord General Cromwell', and the dream-elegy 'Methought I saw my late espoused saint'.
plot_or_argument: Rather than a love sequence, the sonnets treat vocation, blindness, public service, religious persecution, friendship, and loss, each an argument or meditation resolved in the closing lines.
narrative_structure: A non-sequential collection of occasional and meditative sonnets, unified by Milton's concern with duty, faith, and his poetic calling.
principal_characters: the poet; Patience (in 'On His Blindness'); various dedicatees (Cromwell, Vane, Fairfax)
meter_and_prosody: The Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet with Miltonic enjambment and a grand, sonorous syntax that overflows the traditional divisions.
historical_context: Composed from about 1630 to the 1650s–60s; most were published in the 1673 Poems, and they record Milton's engagement with the Civil Wars, the Commonwealth, his blindness, and personal bereavement.
literary_significance: Milton restored the sonnet to serious public and moral use, breaking from the Elizabethan love sequence and influencing Wordsworth and the modern sonnet ('Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour').
bibliographical_notes: Most first printed in Poems (1673). Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Paradise Lost
description: Milton's epic of the Fall of Man in blank verse: Satan's rebellion and expulsion from heaven, his voyage to the new world to corrupt God's creatures, the temptation of Adam and Eve, and their expulsion from Eden — 'to justify the ways of God to men'. Published in ten books (1667) and reissued in twelve (1674).
plot_or_argument: Satan, cast into hell, rallies the fallen angels, volunteers to explore the new world, seduces Eve through the serpent, and Adam falls with her through love; the Son pronounces judgment, Michael shows Adam the future of mankind, and the pair leave Paradise 'hand in hand' with providence their guide.
narrative_structure: An epic in twelve books with invocations, in medias res opening, councils in heaven and hell, extended similes, and a vast temporal and cosmic scope, drawing on classical epic and biblical narrative.
principal_characters: Satan; Adam; Eve; God the Father; the Son; Raphael; Michael; Beelzebub; Sin and Death
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter (blank verse), with Milton's 'sense variously drawn out from one verse into another' and a Latinate grandeur of diction and syntax.
historical_context: Composed chiefly after the Restoration (c. 1658–65), when Milton was blind, politically defeated, and in danger; dictated to amanuenses and published in 1667, it transposes the failed republican cause into a theodicy of obedience, liberty, and inner paradise.
literary_significance: The greatest epic in the English language and a central work of world literature; it shaped English poetry, theology, and political imagination for centuries and inspired responses from Blake and Shelley to modern criticism.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1667 (10 books); second edition 1674 (12 books, with 'The Verse' note on blank verse). Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Paradise Regained
description: Milton's 'brief epic' in four books, retelling the temptation of Christ in the wilderness (Luke 4): Jesus resists Satan's offers of bread, wealth, empire, and classical learning through patient faith and reasoned constancy, thereby regaining Paradise lost through Adam.
plot_or_argument: Satan, disguised, tempts the fasting Christ first with hunger, then with the kingdoms of the world and the glory of Athens; Christ refuses each, exposing Satan's false values, and stands unshaken on the pinnacle of the temple, whereupon Satan is confounded and angels minister to him.
narrative_structure: A dialogue-driven brief epic in blank verse, structured as a series of debates and temptations rather than action, with an austere, argumentative style.
principal_characters: Jesus (the Son); Satan; the disciples; Mary
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, more austere and restrained than Paradise Lost, suited to the patient heroism of 'the better fortitude / Of patience and heroic martyrdom'.
historical_context: Composed after Paradise Lost and published with Samson Agonistes in 1671; it reflects Milton's post-Restoration meditation on true heroism as inner, spiritual constancy rather than martial glory.
literary_significance: A deliberately quiet, intellectual counterpart to Paradise Lost that redefines the epic hero as the patient, obedient Christ; long undervalued, it is now admired for its severity and argumentative power.
bibliographical_notes: Published with Samson Agonistes, 1671. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Samson Agonistes
description: A Greek tragedy in English on the blind Hebrew hero Samson, written to be read rather than performed: imprisoned and blinded by the Philistines, Samson moves from despair to renewed faith and, at the feast of Dagon, pulls down the temple, destroying himself and his enemies in an act of divine vengeance.
plot_or_argument: Samson laments his blindness and capture; he is visited in turn by the Chorus of Danites, his father Manoah, his wife Dalila, and the giant Harapha; summoned to make sport before the Philistine lords at the temple of Dagon, he prays for strength, topples the pillars, and dies triumphantly with his enemies.
narrative_structure: A classical drama observing the unities of time and place, with chorus, stichomythia, messenger, and catharsis, modeled on Sophocles and Aeschylus.
principal_characters: Samson; the Chorus of Danites; Manoah; Dalila; Harapha; the Philistine Officer; the Messenger
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with choruses in varied lyric meters, using the Greek tragic forms of strophe and antistrophe.
historical_context: Published with Paradise Regained in 1671; the blinded, politically defeated hero has long been read as a figure of Milton himself after the Restoration, and the play engages the problem of violent divine justice.
literary_significance: The greatest English example of classical closet tragedy, it fuses Greek form with Hebrew subject and Milton's own condition, and has generated sustained debate about its violence, its politics, and its catharsis.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the title page notes it was 'never intended' for the stage.
bibliographical_notes: Published with Paradise Regained, 1671. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Areopagitica
alternative_titles: Areopagitica: A Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc'd Printing
description: Milton's prose speech to Parliament (24 November 1644) against the Licensing Order of 1643, arguing that prior censorship of books destroys learning, virtue, and truth, and that a free people must be trusted to choose good over evil — the classic English defence of freedom of the press.
plot_or_argument: Milton traces the history of licensing from the Inquisition, argues that books contain the 'life-blood of a master spirit', distinguishes the testing of virtue from its seclusion, and contends that truth will prevail in a free and open encounter.
narrative_structure: A classical oration in prose, modeled on Isocrates's Areopagiticus, moving through historical example, argument, and eloquent peroration.
meter_and_prosody: Eloquent, Latinate prose with a powerful oratorical rhythm and dense classical allusion.
historical_context: Published during the Civil War against Parliament's 1643 licensing order; it drew on Milton's own experience of unlicensed publication and the collapse of censorship.
literary_significance: One of the foundational texts of the argument for free speech and a free press, still quoted in constitutional and press-freedom debates, and a masterpiece of English prose.
bibliographical_notes: Published 1644. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce
alternative_titles: The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce: Restor'd to the Good of Both Sexes
description: Milton's controversial tract arguing that incompatibility, not merely adultery, is grounds for divorce, prompted by his own unhappy marriage to Mary Powell; it defends companionship and 'meet and happy conversation' as the true end of marriage against a rigid scriptural literalism.
plot_or_argument: Milton argues from scripture, reason, and natural law that marriage exists for mutual help and companionship, and that an uncongenial union frustrates its divine purpose, warranting divorce and remarriage.
narrative_structure: A two-book argumentative treatise in prose, with scriptural exegesis and appeals to reason and natural law.
meter_and_prosody: Dense, passionate argumentative prose, at once learned and personal.
historical_context: Written in 1643–44 after Mary Powell left Milton; it scandalised the Presbyterians and led directly to Areopagitica when Milton published without a licence, and to his later tract Tetrachordon (1645).
literary_significance: A landmark in the history of marriage and divorce debate and an important document of Milton's radical Protestant individualism; it also occasioned his defence of unlicensed printing.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1643, expanded 1644. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Of Education
description: A letter to the educational reformer Samuel Hartlib proposing a complete humanist and practical curriculum for young gentlemen, combining classical languages, science, physical training, and moral and religious formation to fit them for public and private service.
plot_or_argument: Milton sets out the ends of education ('to repair the ruins of our first parents by regaining to know God aright'), then details a graded curriculum from languages through literature, science, ethics, and rhetoric, with exercises, travel, and music.
narrative_structure: A short prose tract addressed as a letter, moving from first principles to a detailed syllabus.
meter_and_prosody: Clear, argumentative prose with an idealistic and practical tone.
historical_context: Written in 1644 for Samuel Hartlib's circle of educational reformers, reflecting Comenian and humanist ideals and Milton's own experience as a schoolmaster and private tutor.
literary_significance: A key document of seventeenth-century educational reform, combining Renaissance humanism with the new practical and scientific emphasis, and influential in the history of pedagogy.
bibliographical_notes: Published 1644. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates
alternative_titles: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates: Proving That It Is Lawful ... to Call to Account a Tyrant, King or Magistrate
description: Milton's republican tract, published weeks after the execution of Charles I, arguing that sovereignty originates in the people, that kings are the people's servants, and that it is lawful to depose and execute a tyrant — a defence of regicide and popular sovereignty.
plot_or_argument: Milton argues from scripture, classical authority, and the law of nations that magistrates hold power by the people's trust, that a tyrant forfeits it, and that the people may judge and punish him, defending the Army's act against Presbyterian critics.
narrative_structure: A polemical prose treatise of sustained argument, moving from political theory to the immediate justification of the regicide.
meter_and_prosody: Forceful, learned, argumentative prose with a fierce polemical edge.
historical_context: Written in February 1649 immediately after Charles I's execution, partly to answer Presbyterians who had supported the war but recoiled from regicide; it secured Milton his post as Latin Secretary to the Commonwealth.
literary_significance: A foundational text of republican political theory and resistance doctrine, influencing later Whig and revolutionary thought in England and America.
bibliographical_notes: First edition February 1649, expanded 1650. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Eikonoklastes
alternative_titles: Eikonoklastes: In Answer to a Book Intitl'd Eikon Basilike
description: Milton's point-by-point rebuttal of the Eikon Basilike, the hugely popular devotional memoir attributed to the martyred Charles I; as 'the image-breaker' (eikonoklastes), Milton dismantles the royalist cult of the king's suffering and exposes the book's political purposes.
plot_or_argument: Following the chapters of the Eikon Basilike, Milton answers each pious self-portrait of the king with argument, scriptural counter-example, and political critique, denying Charles the status of martyr and the book its authority.
narrative_structure: A chapter-by-chapter refutation in prose, mirroring and dismantling the structure of the royalist book it answers.
meter_and_prosody: Sustained, ironic, and forceful argumentative prose.
historical_context: Commissioned by the Commonwealth in 1649 to counter the immense popularity of the Eikon Basilike; it forms part of Milton's official defence of the regicide alongside The Tenure.
literary_significance: A central text of the Eikon Basilike controversy and of Civil War print propaganda, important for understanding the battle over Charles I's image and the culture of polemic.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name by order of the Council of State.
bibliographical_notes: Published 1649. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: Defensio Pro Populo Anglicano
description: Milton's Latin defence of the English Commonwealth and the regicide, answering the Defensio Regia of Claudius Salmasius; written for a European audience in his capacity as Latin Secretary, it vindicates popular sovereignty and the English people against royalist propaganda abroad.
plot_or_argument: Milton refutes Salmasius's defence of monarchy and attack on the regicide point by point, arguing that kings are accountable to the people, that tyrants may be judged, and that the English republic is lawful and honourable.
narrative_structure: A learned Latin polemic of sustained argument, structured as a rebuttal of Salmasius's treatise.
meter_and_prosody: Eloquent, erudite Latin prose with powerful oratorical and satirical force.
historical_context: Commissioned by the Council of State in 1650 and published in 1651; Milton's exertion on it (while already losing his sight) is said to have hastened his total blindness, and it earned him European fame.
literary_significance: The most important Latin political work of the English Revolution, defending republicanism to the continent and establishing Milton's international reputation as a political thinker.
bibliographical_notes: Published 1651 (Latin); English translation 1692. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).

title: The Ready and Easy Way to Establish a Free Commonwealth
description: Milton's last political tract, published in two editions in the desperate weeks before the Restoration, proposing a perpetual senate and constitutional safeguards to preserve a free republic and avert the return of monarchy, in a tone of prophetic warning and undaunted republican faith.
plot_or_argument: Milton argues for a self-perpetuating ruling council (with local government and a 'grand council'), warns of the dangers and moral degradation of restoring the Stuarts, and urges his countrymen not to throw away the fruits of the Revolution.
narrative_structure: A political pamphlet in two editions (February and April 1660), combining constitutional proposal with urgent exhortation.
meter_and_prosody: Passionate, prophetic, argumentative prose of a man writing against certain defeat.
historical_context: Written in early 1660 as General Monck moved to restore the monarchy; the second edition appeared only weeks before Charles II's return, when publication was an act of considerable personal danger.
literary_significance: Milton's final and most poignant republican statement, a constitutional proposal and a testament of unyielding commitment to liberty in the face of imminent defeat.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name at great personal risk.
bibliographical_notes: Two editions, February and April 1660. Standard edition: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton (Modern Library, 2007).
